item.title: The Daily Star – From Airbus to energy: The expanding Bangladesh–France partnership
item.description:
Jean-Marc Séré-Charlet, French Ambassador to Bangladesh, speaks to The Daily Star about the evolving Bangladesh–France partnership, opportunities to expand bilateral trade and investment, Bangladesh’s economic diversification and LDC graduation, cooperation in renewable energy, higher education and the Indo-Pacific, longstanding cultural ties, and France’s perspective on Bangladesh’s democratic transition and institutional reforms.

The Daily Star (TDS): France has recently seen student-led protests over government policies and political accountability. How do you assess the grievances behind these demonstrations and the government's response?

Jean-Marc Séré-Charlet (JMSC): France has a long tradition of demonstrations. The French Revolution itself began with demonstrations, and the right to demonstrate is protected by our Constitution. People must be free to exercise this right and call for change.

What matters is that legitimate demonstrations remain free from violence. We have seen small groups join protests to loot or cause disturbances rather than express legitimate demands. Following the serious outbreak of violence on 17 October, the government had to address the law-and-order situation while allowing people to continue demonstrating.

TDS: This year marks the 50th death anniversary of André Malraux, who supported Bangladesh's Liberation War in 1971. How can France and Bangladesh build on their historical and cultural ties to strengthen cooperation in culture, education and people-to-people exchanges?

JMSC: Culture is central to our cooperation. France values its heritage, arts and creativity, and began protecting its heritage through legislation as early as 1830s. André Malraux, our first minister of culture, reflected that commitment. We want to share it with our partners.

Our cultural relationship with Bangladesh goes back a long way. The Alliance Française in Dhaka was established in 1959, and the one in Chittagong in 1965. These are places where our cultures meet, and the exchanges predate Bangladesh's independence.

We have government-to-government agreements on cultural cooperation and archaeology. Recently, curators from Bangladesh spent two months at the Musée du Quai Branly in Paris. They shared experiences with their French counterparts. We want more such exchanges.

I would also include higher education in this wider understanding of culture. We want students and researchers from both countries to meet and work together. We already have Bangladeshi students in France, but we hope to welcome more. Student exchanges are a long-term investment because they help our societies understand each other better.
Jean-Marc Séré-Charlet, French Ambassador to Bangladesh

TDS: France is an important European market for Bangladesh's ready-made garments, while Biman's decision to purchase Airbus aircraft marks a new chapter in bilateral economic relations. What opportunities do you see for expanding trade, attracting French investment and diversifying Bangladesh's exports?

JMSC: First, the Airbus agreement is a success, but it is important to recognise that it is Biman's own strategic decision. The discussions began years ago at Biman's request. The airline wanted a mixed fleet to strengthen its autonomy rather than depend on one supplier. Many international airlines operate both Airbus and Boeing aircraft.

The choice of the A350-900 is significant because of its range. It would give Biman the capacity to operate directly from Dhaka to the east coast of the United States without a stop. Aircraft purchases create partnerships that last much longer than a year or two.

We see great potential in Bangladesh. French companies are impressed by the quality and responsiveness of its ready-made garment industry. Many French consumers buy Bangladeshi clothes without knowing where they were made. Even when I buy clothes for my children, I often notice that they come from Bangladesh. French companies know the industry well.

The challenge is diversification. The ‘Everything But Arms’ arrangement has given Bangladesh valuable access to the European market, but there are opportunities beyond garments, including pharmaceuticals and more technical industries. French companies would be interested in sourcing from Bangladesh if those sectors were developed further. Ultimately, that depends on Bangladeshi businesses and the government's choices. The period before LDC graduation is an important opportunity to improve competitiveness, diversify production and make Bangladesh better known internationally.

TDS: President Emmanuel Macron's visit to Bangladesh in September 2023 gave fresh momentum to bilateral relations. How has the partnership evolved since then, and which areas should receive greater attention in the coming years?

JMSC: France and Bangladesh have been partners since 1972, so this relationship is much older than the last three years. André Malraux supported Bangladesh even before it became independent. President Macron's visit is part of a much longer relationship that we want to develop further.

More than 1.5 million French citizens live permanently in the Indo-Pacific region. We are both Indo-Pacific countries and face common challenges in maritime affairs, the blue economy, biodiversity and climate resilience.

We also want to help Bangladesh strengthen its sovereignty in important sectors. We have cooperation in satellites and space technology, including Bangladesh Satellite-1, which is a Franco-Bangladeshi satellite, as well as civil aviation and communications. Civil aviation matters because a country needs the capacity to connect with the world rather than depending entirely on other countries’ airlines. We are also in discussions about working together to combat human trafficking. The French Development Agency has also been active here for 15 years.

My mission is to create stronger links between our societies. We want this relationship to become closer through practical cooperations and continued exchanges.
On 19 September 1971, Paris Jour published a declaration by André Malraux expressing his intention to participate in Bangladesh’s Liberation War.

TDS: France has supported Bangladesh's energy transition through financing and technical cooperation. How can the two countries deepen their partnership in renewable energy, energy efficiency and modernising power infrastructure?

JMSC: Greener energy is a shared challenge for Bangladesh, France and other countries. We are working on this transition at home and with partners such as Bangladesh.

The French Development Agency has supported the energy transition through credit lines, including €100 million for IDCOL (Infrastructure Development Company Limited) and €50 million for BIFFL (Bangladesh Infrastructure Finance Fund Limited). These arrangements help private companies invest in energy efficiency and renewable energy generation at their own facilities.

We have also worked with Dhaka Power Distribution Company, with 40 new substations installed since 2015. In addition, we are involved in a smart-grid pilot funded by the European Union to improve the efficiency of the distribution network. We want concrete projects, not just statements.

We would like to bring more French expertise to Bangladesh and encourage French energy companies to explore opportunities here. But companies also need better market access and a more favourable business environment. These conditions will help us to convince companies to enter the market.

TDS: At the October 2026 Bay of Bengal Conversation, you noted that formal negotiations on an EU–Bangladesh free trade agreement had yet to begin. With Bangladesh approaching LDC graduation, what would be necessary to initiate negotiations and ensure a mutually beneficial agreement?

JMSC: At the Bay of Bengal Conversation, I stated a fact: formal negotiations have not yet started. The European Union has clearly heard Bangladesh's wish to open negotiations on a free trade agreement. Such negotiations require careful preparation and can take some time.

EU members must first establish whether there is a common interest in negotiations. The 27 member states then prepare their positions and agree on a mandate for the European Commission, which will conduct the negotiations. That process takes time.

An agreement must serve the interests of both partners. We understand that low tariffs are essential for Bangladesh and that preferential access has helped Bangladeshi exports grow in Europe over the past 25 years. But we also want European businesses to have good conditions in which to operate in the Bangladeshi market. At a minimum, they should receive treatment equal to that offered to Bangladesh's other partners.

A balanced agreement does not necessarily mean identical concessions, because the two economies and their products are different. It does mean that each side must benefit. 
French President Emmanuel Macron’s historic visit to Dhaka in September 2023 was the first by a French president to Bangladesh in more than three decades and marked a milestone in bilateral relations. Photo: PID

TDS: As an Indo-Pacific power, France has significant strategic interests in the region, while Bangladesh occupies an important position in the Bay of Bengal. How do you envision greater bilateral cooperation in maritime affairs, the blue economy and regional stability amid growing geopolitical competition?

JMSC: France is an Indo-Pacific country, with more than 1.5 million French citizens living permanently in the region. With Bangladesh, we face common challenges.

Maritime issues, the blue economy and the protection of biodiversity are areas in which we want to strengthen our cooperation. Climate resilience and mitigation are also important. We want closer ties and to help Bangladesh strengthen its capabilities in key sectors.

We believe strongly in multilateralism and cooperation rather than confrontation. We are concerned by what we see as the growing brutalisation of the world. This does not benefit poorer people, whose interests matter too. We want to build our relationship through dialogue and cooperation.

TDS: Bangladesh has a large young population, while France has internationally recognised universities and research institutions. What opportunities exist to expand student exchanges, academic partnerships and joint research between the two countries?

JMSC: Bangladesh has a large student population, and training is essential. Going abroad is a very good way to learn and to broaden one's outlook. We encourage our own students in France to spend at least one year abroad during their studies.

France has major universities and research institutions, and we would like to develop much closer links between them and their Bangladeshi counterparts. Research depends on international exchanges of ideas and experience.

We have already had French researchers working with Bangladeshi colleagues on longer-term projects, and we would welcome more exchanges in both directions. We want more Bangladeshi students in France and more French researchers working with institutions in Bangladesh.

There is a service at our embassy dedicated to developing these contacts. I have asked our cultural team to make this a priority. We need to identify the right institutions and people on both sides so that cooperation can grow. These exchanges help build mutual understanding over the long term.
The launch of Bangladesh’s first satellite, Bangabandhu-1, manufactured in France by the Franco-Italian aerospace company Thales Alenia Space under a turnkey contract with Bangladesh. Photo: Wikipedia

TDS: Following Bangladesh's 2024 student-led uprising and the February 2026 elections, the country is navigating a period of democratic transition and institutional reform. How does France view this process, and what role can France and the European Union play in supporting democratic institutions, human rights and good governance?

JMSC: What happened in Bangladesh demonstrates the people's commitment to democracy and their determination to defend it. But democracy is a long journey. Following the February 2026 elections, there are still important reforms to pursue.

These include strengthening the independence of the judiciary and fighting corruption so that the benefits of government services actually reach the people. Respect for human rights must also be guaranteed through adequate institutions. Freedom of expression and freedom of the media are essential pillars of democracy.

The government has told us it wants to make progress, and we will follow these reforms with interest. Of course, the decisions belong to the government and people of Bangladesh. France and the European Union would be happy to share our experience and expertise, while respecting that responsibility.

One example is the European Union's election observation mission. Bangladesh asked the EU to send observers, and around 200 European observers came. It was a considerable commitment, and we believed it would support Bangladesh's democratic process. This is the kind of practical exchange we would like to continue. 

The interview was taken by Ystiaque Ahmed and Khairul Hasan Jahin.

item.title: The Daily Star – ICJ judgment against Myanmar : Can it bring justice to the Rohingya and relief to Bangladesh?
item.description:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) issued its final judgment on 19 November 2026 in a case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar under the 1948 Genocide Convention. The Court found Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya people in 2017. The Gambia filed the case in 2019. It won a unanimous provisional measures order in January 2020 and a near-unanimous ruling upholding the Court’s jurisdiction in July 2022. The merits hearings closed in January 2026. Myanmar denies the accusations and says its 2017 offensive was a legitimate counter-terrorism campaign. More than 730,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh during that campaign, around 400 villages were fully or partially burnt, 10,000 people were killed, and 1,900 women and girls were raped, according to the UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission reports published in 2018. The Gambia presented all these documents at the ICJ’s hearings to counter Myanmar’s “counter-insurgency” arguments. After scrutinising all the documents, victims’ testimonies, arguments and counter-arguments, and circumstantial evidence, the Court issued an 11-point judgment declaring Myanmar a state responsible for committing genocide. This article presents a critical analysis of the consequences the ICJ’s judgment will have on the ground for the Rohingya people, as well as its implications for Bangladesh, Myanmar and the international community.

What it means for the Rohingya

The Rohingya have been denied citizenship, freedom of movement and even their name for years, as they are officially called “Bengalis” in Myanmar. Firstly, the ICJ’s judgment declared that what Myanmar did to the Rohingya in 2017 was carried out with an “intent to destroy” them as a group; it brought genuine justice to the victims. The verdict held the perpetrator accountable and also recognised Rohingya identity and ethnicity, settling a long-overdue debate. Official denial at the state level allows persecution to continue, and the World Court’s decision has substantially undermined Myanmar’s version of Rohingya existence.

Secondly, the judgment would strengthen the legal basis for a durable solution. Since the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, the judgment places an international legal obligation on Myanmar to stop ongoing abuses, prevent any further persecution, provide compensation and offer rehabilitation. The judgment would help create the conditions for safe and dignified Rohingya repatriation. It would also give the Rohingya, Bangladesh and the UN solid legal grounds to argue for the Rohingya’s return with citizenship, safety and dignity, because Myanmar is solely responsible for their displacement.

Thirdly, the ICJ’s judgment will make a significant difference for the Rohingya who remain in Rakhine State. In its order on ‘provisional measures’, the Court had already ordered Myanmar to stop further ‘acts of genocide’ and to preserve ‘genocidal evidence’; the final judgment provides stronger grounds for protecting the Rohingya in Rakhine State. Because the Court accepted The Gambia’s claims, this is the first ICJ judgment to link sexual and gender-based violence to genocide, which helps strengthen the 1948 Genocide Convention and the 1998 Rome Statute. In this sense, the judgment will bring justice to rape victims by establishing that sexual abuse is not merely a side effect of genocide but a deliberate method of destruction, forming part of the “intent to destroy”.

However, the judgment will not bring rapid change, as the Court has no power to enforce its decisions directly. It offers hope, courage and legal grounds, but little immediate help; action will take longer.
A Rohingya refugee takes a selfie while the verdict is translated for the gathered crowd watching the live announcement by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the minority Rohingya population, on a big screen at a refugee camp in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, November 19, 2026. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain

How Bangladesh would benefit

Bangladesh is not directly involved in the case, but it has taken on much of the ‘burden’ by hosting over 1.2 million refugees and shouldering the economic costs, environmental challenges, security issues and social tensions in and near the camps. The Court’s judgment will help Bangladesh in several ways.

Firstly, the ICJ’s judgment would strengthen Bangladesh’s diplomatic bargaining position as host to a huge Rohingya refugee population. Dhaka has been dealing with the Rohingya issue in search of a political solution; the judgment turns the crisis from a political question into a legal fact. With the judgment as a legal basis, Bangladesh can argue that Myanmar is responsible for the mass exodus and that it is Myanmar’s duty to bring the Rohingya back. Bangladesh provided shelter as an act of generosity for the sake of humanity, not as a permanent responsibility to host more than 1.2 million refugees. 

After the 2022 ICJ ruling on jurisdiction, Bangladesh’s then foreign ministry said that accountability was key to a durable solution and helped build trust for voluntary, safe and dignified repatriation. The final judgment makes this argument even stronger, which would help Rohingya repatriation. Efforts at repatriation have stalled since 2021, mainly because Rakhine remains unsafe due to Myanmar’s political instability, the ongoing civil war and the increasing dominance of the Arakan Army in the region. With the judgment, Bangladesh could urge India, China, Japan and ASEAN countries to see safe return as a legal and moral duty.

Secondly, beyond repatriation talks, the judgment will give Bangladesh greater leverage in seeking donor support at a time when a shrinking international support base is putting pressure on its economy. Recent global crises, particularly the Russia–Ukraine war, the Israel–Palestine conflict and the ongoing Iran–US conflict, have strained the world economy and affected donors’ support for Rohingya humanitarian assistance. A decline in international humanitarian support puts pressure on Bangladesh and reduces the quality of life for Rohingya in Bangladesh. With the judgment, Bangladesh could argue more forcefully to Western and Gulf donors that funding the camps is about upholding a World Court decision, not just charity and humanitarian aid.

Thirdly, the Rohingya camps in Bangladesh have gradually become a serious threat to local and regional ‘security’ and political stability because of infighting, killings, abductions, human trafficking, illegal border trade and arms trafficking. Long-term camp life leads to insecurity, trafficking, risks of ‘radicalisation’ and tensions with local communities in Cox’s Bazar. The verdict would bring a realistic chance for the Rohingya to return, which could help Bangladesh address these security and stability problems through repatriation.
Myanmar's Union Minister for the Ministry of the President's Office Ko Ko Hlaing attends a hearing on the day the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivers its judgment in the case brought by Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority, in The Hague, Netherlands, November 19, 2026. REUTERS/Piroschka van de Wouw

Yet Bangladesh’s expectations should be realistic, since the ICJ’s judgment cannot compel any country to accept returning refugees when political conditions in Myanmar are neither stable nor suitable for the Rohingya to return. Dhaka will gain legal grounds from the verdict for a stronger voice at the negotiating table and, with support, for persuading the international community, but the ICJ has hardly any power to enforce its judgment.

Consequences for Myanmar

The ICJ’s finding that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017 will have huge legal and political consequences for the country. Myanmar would have to immediately end any ongoing persecution and make due reparations as ordered by the ICJ (points 9, 10 and 11 of the judgment). Though the ICJ did not set an exact amount, it ordered compensation, and Myanmar might have to compensate the Rohingya within two years. As Myanmar is a party to the Genocide Convention and is subject to the Court’s jurisdiction, it is legally bound by the ruling.

The damage to Myanmar’s international image could last even longer than the legal consequences. The genocide finding will make it difficult for Myanmar, its military and even a future government to regain international trust and restore its reputation. As a country found to have committed genocide, Myanmar will find it harder to engage in arms sales, regional partnerships, global forums, foreign investment, diplomatic relations, and bilateral as well as multilateral trade. 

The judgment could lead to further sanctions and calls for action against military-linked businesses, investments and corporate deals. Though the ICJ cannot send generals to jail or enforce its judgment directly and immediately, the judgment provides strong grounds for holding generals to account, as perpetrators can be prosecuted by other bodies, such as the International Criminal Court or national courts like those in Argentina.

The big problem lies in the system: enforcement of the ICJ’s judgment largely depends on the UN Security Council, where Myanmar’s allies, China and Russia, can protect it. Myanmar could also ignore the judgment, as some countries have done before. However, disregarding a final ICJ judgment comes at a cost, as it leaves a country more isolated in its defiance of international law.
Rohingya refugees watch the live announcement of a verdict by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the minority Rohingya population, on a big screen at a refugee camp in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, November 19, 2026. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain

The international impact of the ICJ judgment

Beyond its implications for the Rohingya, Bangladesh and Myanmar, the ICJ’s judgment will have a far-reaching global impact.

Firstly, the Court’s judgment sets an unprecedented example by showing that a third party can bring a case to seek justice for victims. The Court’s only previous genocide judgments on the merits involved Bosnia, where Serbia was found to have failed to prevent and punish genocide but was not deemed directly responsible, and Croatia v. Serbia, in which no genocide was established. This judgment is historic because it is the first time the ICJ has found a state responsible for committing genocide. It will also show how “intent” can be revealed through patterns of behaviour, how to address sexual violence and community annihilation, and what evidence is needed. These points set a precedent to guide future genocide cases. Some experts have already said this judgment could set a remarkable precedent for other genocide cases, such as South Africa’s case against Israel over the war in Gaza.

Secondly, the judgment confirms an important principle: any country that is a party to the Genocide Convention can act to enforce it, even if it was not directly harmed or affected. The Gambia, a small West African country, has no direct connection to the Rohingya genocide but lodged this case with the active support of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). The judgment shows that preventing genocide is the responsibility not only of directly affected countries but of every country that is a party to the 1948 Genocide Convention. It would motivate other small countries, despite their less powerful position in global power politics, to step forward and bring cases concerning genocide.

Thirdly, the ICJ’s judgment will call into question the integrity of the international system. The Rohingya have been suffering for decades, but the world has taken no real action beyond helping them survive without a meaningful life. The judgment will put pressure on states that support Myanmar’s military. It would also reshape discussions about targeted sanctions, arms embargoes and the limits of the Security Council veto.

Finally, and most importantly, the ICJ’s judgment will challenge the culture of impunity that serves global power, geopolitics and corporate interests. Even if the implementation and enforcement of the judgment take time, it conveys a clear message that evidence can accumulate and accountability can eventually follow, even for powerful militaries that act in secret.
A house is seen on fire in Gawduthar village, Maungdaw township, in the north of Rakhine state, Myanmar September 7, 2017. Photo: REUTERS

Conclusion

The ICJ’s judgment of 19 November will not immediately heal the Rohingya’s wounds, ease their brutal pain or rescue them from the trauma of genocide, but it will hold the perpetrators accountable and bring justice to the victims. The ICJ cannot rebuild destroyed villages, secure the Rohingya’s legal recognition as Myanmar’s citizens or bring them back overnight. Yet it can establish the truth in law, give victims recognised legal standing, strengthen Bangladesh’s diplomatic position, place lasting stigma and legal obligations on Myanmar, and show the world that perpetrators of genocide can be held to account. Whether this leads to a safe return, reparations and real accountability will depend on how states, especially Myanmar’s neighbours, supporters, regional allies and international partners, respond to the judgment. Nonetheless, the ICJ’s judgment on the Rohingya genocide is a historic landmark and an example of upholding the spirit and ideals of global justice in the 21st century.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) issued its final judgment on 19 November 2026 in a case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar under the 1948 Genocide Convention. The Court found Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya people in 2017. The Gambia filed the case in 2019. It won a unanimous provisional measures order in January 2020 and a near-unanimous ruling upholding the Court’s jurisdiction in July 2022. The merits hearings closed in January 2026. Myanmar denies the accusations and says its 2017 offensive was a legitimate counter-terrorism campaign. More than 730,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh during that campaign, around 400 villages were fully or partially burnt, 10,000 people were killed, and 1,900 women and girls were raped, according to the UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission reports published in 2018. The Gambia presented all these documents at the ICJ’s hearings to counter Myanmar’s “counter-insurgency” arguments. After scrutinising all the documents, victims’ testimonies, arguments and counter-arguments, and circumstantial evidence, the Court issued an 11-point judgment declaring Myanmar a state responsible for committing genocide. This article presents a critical analysis of the consequences the ICJ’s judgment will have on the ground for the Rohingya people, as well as its implications for Bangladesh, Myanmar and the international community.

What it means for the Rohingya

The Rohingya have been denied citizenship, freedom of movement and even their name for years, as they are officially called “Bengalis” in Myanmar. Firstly, the ICJ’s judgment declared that what Myanmar did to the Rohingya in 2017 was carried out with an “intent to destroy” them as a group; it brought genuine justice to the victims. The verdict held the perpetrator accountable and also recognised Rohingya identity and ethnicity, settling a long-overdue debate. Official denial at the state level allows persecution to continue, and the World Court’s decision has substantially undermined Myanmar’s version of Rohingya existence.

Secondly, the judgment would strengthen the legal basis for a durable solution. Since the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, the judgment places an international legal obligation on Myanmar to stop ongoing abuses, prevent any further persecution, provide compensation and offer rehabilitation. The judgment would help create the conditions for safe and dignified Rohingya repatriation. It would also give the Rohingya, Bangladesh and the UN solid legal grounds to argue for the Rohingya’s return with citizenship, safety and dignity, because Myanmar is solely responsible for their displacement.

Thirdly, the ICJ’s judgment will make a significant difference for the Rohingya who remain in Rakhine State. In its order on ‘provisional measures’, the Court had already ordered Myanmar to stop further ‘acts of genocide’ and to preserve ‘genocidal evidence’; the final judgment provides stronger grounds for protecting the Rohingya in Rakhine State. Because the Court accepted The Gambia’s claims, this is the first ICJ judgment to link sexual and gender-based violence to genocide, which helps strengthen the 1948 Genocide Convention and the 1998 Rome Statute. In this sense, the judgment will bring justice to rape victims by establishing that sexual abuse is not merely a side effect of genocide but a deliberate method of destruction, forming part of the “intent to destroy”.

However, the judgment will not bring rapid change, as the Court has no power to enforce its decisions directly. It offers hope, courage and legal grounds, but little immediate help; action will take longer.
A Rohingya refugee takes a selfie while the verdict is translated for the gathered crowd watching the live announcement by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the minority Rohingya population, on a big screen at a refugee camp in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, November 19, 2026. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain

How Bangladesh would benefit

Bangladesh is not directly involved in the case, but it has taken on much of the ‘burden’ by hosting over 1.2 million refugees and shouldering the economic costs, environmental challenges, security issues and social tensions in and near the camps. The Court’s judgment will help Bangladesh in several ways.

Firstly, the ICJ’s judgment would strengthen Bangladesh’s diplomatic bargaining position as host to a huge Rohingya refugee population. Dhaka has been dealing with the Rohingya issue in search of a political solution; the judgment turns the crisis from a political question into a legal fact. With the judgment as a legal basis, Bangladesh can argue that Myanmar is responsible for the mass exodus and that it is Myanmar’s duty to bring the Rohingya back. Bangladesh provided shelter as an act of generosity for the sake of humanity, not as a permanent responsibility to host more than 1.2 million refugees. 

After the 2022 ICJ ruling on jurisdiction, Bangladesh’s then foreign ministry said that accountability was key to a durable solution and helped build trust for voluntary, safe and dignified repatriation. The final judgment makes this argument even stronger, which would help Rohingya repatriation. Efforts at repatriation have stalled since 2021, mainly because Rakhine remains unsafe due to Myanmar’s political instability, the ongoing civil war and the increasing dominance of the Arakan Army in the region. With the judgment, Bangladesh could urge India, China, Japan and ASEAN countries to see safe return as a legal and moral duty.

Secondly, beyond repatriation talks, the judgment will give Bangladesh greater leverage in seeking donor support at a time when a shrinking international support base is putting pressure on its economy. Recent global crises, particularly the Russia–Ukraine war, the Israel–Palestine conflict and the ongoing Iran–US conflict, have strained the world economy and affected donors’ support for Rohingya humanitarian assistance. A decline in international humanitarian support puts pressure on Bangladesh and reduces the quality of life for Rohingya in Bangladesh. With the judgment, Bangladesh could argue more forcefully to Western and Gulf donors that funding the camps is about upholding a World Court decision, not just charity and humanitarian aid.

Thirdly, the Rohingya camps in Bangladesh have gradually become a serious threat to local and regional ‘security’ and political stability because of infighting, killings, abductions, human trafficking, illegal border trade and arms trafficking. Long-term camp life leads to insecurity, trafficking, risks of ‘radicalisation’ and tensions with local communities in Cox’s Bazar. The verdict would bring a realistic chance for the Rohingya to return, which could help Bangladesh address these security and stability problems through repatriation.
Myanmar's Union Minister for the Ministry of the President's Office Ko Ko Hlaing attends a hearing on the day the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivers its judgment in the case brought by Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority, in The Hague, Netherlands, November 19, 2026. REUTERS/Piroschka van de Wouw

Yet Bangladesh’s expectations should be realistic, since the ICJ’s judgment cannot compel any country to accept returning refugees when political conditions in Myanmar are neither stable nor suitable for the Rohingya to return. Dhaka will gain legal grounds from the verdict for a stronger voice at the negotiating table and, with support, for persuading the international community, but the ICJ has hardly any power to enforce its judgment.

Consequences for Myanmar

The ICJ’s finding that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017 will have huge legal and political consequences for the country. Myanmar would have to immediately end any ongoing persecution and make due reparations as ordered by the ICJ (points 9, 10 and 11 of the judgment). Though the ICJ did not set an exact amount, it ordered compensation, and Myanmar might have to compensate the Rohingya within two years. As Myanmar is a party to the Genocide Convention and is subject to the Court’s jurisdiction, it is legally bound by the ruling.

The damage to Myanmar’s international image could last even longer than the legal consequences. The genocide finding will make it difficult for Myanmar, its military and even a future government to regain international trust and restore its reputation. As a country found to have committed genocide, Myanmar will find it harder to engage in arms sales, regional partnerships, global forums, foreign investment, diplomatic relations, and bilateral as well as multilateral trade. 

The judgment could lead to further sanctions and calls for action against military-linked businesses, investments and corporate deals. Though the ICJ cannot send generals to jail or enforce its judgment directly and immediately, the judgment provides strong grounds for holding generals to account, as perpetrators can be prosecuted by other bodies, such as the International Criminal Court or national courts like those in Argentina.

The big problem lies in the system: enforcement of the ICJ’s judgment largely depends on the UN Security Council, where Myanmar’s allies, China and Russia, can protect it. Myanmar could also ignore the judgment, as some countries have done before. However, disregarding a final ICJ judgment comes at a cost, as it leaves a country more isolated in its defiance of international law.
Rohingya refugees watch the live announcement of a verdict by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the minority Rohingya population, on a big screen at a refugee camp in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, November 19, 2026. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain

The international impact of the ICJ judgment

Beyond its implications for the Rohingya, Bangladesh and Myanmar, the ICJ’s judgment will have a far-reaching global impact.

Firstly, the Court’s judgment sets an unprecedented example by showing that a third party can bring a case to seek justice for victims. The Court’s only previous genocide judgments on the merits involved Bosnia, where Serbia was found to have failed to prevent and punish genocide but was not deemed directly responsible, and Croatia v. Serbia, in which no genocide was established. This judgment is historic because it is the first time the ICJ has found a state responsible for committing genocide. It will also show how “intent” can be revealed through patterns of behaviour, how to address sexual violence and community annihilation, and what evidence is needed. These points set a precedent to guide future genocide cases. Some experts have already said this judgment could set a remarkable precedent for other genocide cases, such as South Africa’s case against Israel over the war in Gaza.

Secondly, the judgment confirms an important principle: any country that is a party to the Genocide Convention can act to enforce it, even if it was not directly harmed or affected. The Gambia, a small West African country, has no direct connection to the Rohingya genocide but lodged this case with the active support of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). The judgment shows that preventing genocide is the responsibility not only of directly affected countries but of every country that is a party to the 1948 Genocide Convention. It would motivate other small countries, despite their less powerful position in global power politics, to step forward and bring cases concerning genocide.

Thirdly, the ICJ’s judgment will call into question the integrity of the international system. The Rohingya have been suffering for decades, but the world has taken no real action beyond helping them survive without a meaningful life. The judgment will put pressure on states that support Myanmar’s military. It would also reshape discussions about targeted sanctions, arms embargoes and the limits of the Security Council veto.

Finally, and most importantly, the ICJ’s judgment will challenge the culture of impunity that serves global power, geopolitics and corporate interests. Even if the implementation and enforcement of the judgment take time, it conveys a clear message that evidence can accumulate and accountability can eventually follow, even for powerful militaries that act in secret.
A house is seen on fire in Gawduthar village, Maungdaw township, in the north of Rakhine state, Myanmar September 7, 2017. Photo: REUTERS

Conclusion

The ICJ’s judgment of 19 November will not immediately heal the Rohingya’s wounds, ease their brutal pain or rescue them from the trauma of genocide, but it will hold the perpetrators accountable and bring justice to the victims. The ICJ cannot rebuild destroyed villages, secure the Rohingya’s legal recognition as Myanmar’s citizens or bring them back overnight. Yet it can establish the truth in law, give victims recognised legal standing, strengthen Bangladesh’s diplomatic position, place lasting stigma and legal obligations on Myanmar, and show the world that perpetrators of genocide can be held to account. Whether this leads to a safe return, reparations and real accountability will depend on how states, especially Myanmar’s neighbours, supporters, regional allies and international partners, respond to the judgment. Nonetheless, the ICJ’s judgment on the Rohingya genocide is a historic landmark and an example of upholding the spirit and ideals of global justice in the 21st century.

Nasir Uddin is a professor of anthropology at the University of Chittagong and the director of the Refugee and Migration Lab (RML). He is the author of The Rohingya: An Ethnography of ‘Subhuman’ Life (Oxford University Press, 2020). X: @nasiruddincu

item.description:
At DD Art Gallery, the journey of 35 Bangladeshi painters moves from charging animals and straining bodies to rivers, families and love, and finds, at every turn, something luminous holding out against the dark.

A bull, charging. That is the welcome. In Jamal Ahmed’s Bull 2, the animal comes almost straight at the viewer, horns lowered, its body foreshortened into a wedge of force, its back legs dissolving into the dust it kicks up. Nothing in the room that follows quite escapes it. Jamal has hung its twin nearby. In Bull 1, the animal twists rather than charges, one hoof raised, tail whipping out behind it. Together they are two frames of the same second: the turn, then the attack. 
Jamal Ahmed, Bull-1, acrylic on canvas, 60 x 36 inches

A few walls away, Dulal Chandrow Gain's Bull gallops past in profile through a rose-coloured dusk, its hind legs smeared into motion. Jahangir Hossain's horse in Destination leaps toward a red disc at the edge of the canvas, and the half of the picture he has left empty is the distance it still has to cover.

On view at DD Art Gallery until December 3, Art First brings together 35 artists, from the country’s most senior painters to those still early in their careers. The title is a deliberately broad banner. But linger in the room long enough and a more particular story begins to assemble itself. It is worth knowing before you look.

It begins with force: animals and bodies in motion, the restless energy of a place that has always had to move fast to stay alive. Force leaves wounds, and a cluster of works bears witness to them, from a factory collapse to a cracked human face. Beneath both lies the ground that holds people up: families, villages, rivers, old songs. From that ground, the paintings begin to rise, in birds and fish and single flowers holding out against fields of colour. And the show comes to rest, if you let it, in an embrace: two doves meeting in mid-air, and a painter's argument that “love conquers all”.

A few things help along the way. Watch the animals, which change from bulls to egrets to doves as the mood shifts from aggression to grace. Watch the water, which runs through nearly every room. Watch the red, which burns in the angriest pictures and the most tender ones alike. And watch for small things, a hibiscus, a boat, a child's direct gaze, set against something far larger. That is where this show keeps its argument.
Shahabuddin Ahmed, Running, artist-approved print, 36 x 24 inches

Then there is Shahabuddin Ahmed, who has spent a career painting bodies that refuse to keep still. His print Running is a knot of flung limbs, so fast that it is hard to say whether it shows one body or two. By the time I reached it, a red dot on the frame said it had already been sold. His Hanging, printed the same year as Running, shows a muscular back with the arms flung wide and the head dropped between the shoulders. Two slashes of red at the wrists are the only colour. Nearby, in an ornate frame, hangs his Thirst, an oil painting that catches a human figure in raw, desperate motion. It is Shahabuddin at his most recognisable: sweeping, explosive brushstrokes, a narrow palette of fleshy pinks and earthy browns, a pale, almost empty ground. The body seems to be both reaching and coming apart. As so often in his work, struggle and resilience share a single gesture. At its simplest, it shows a body dissolving into paint.

Painters like Rembrandt and Francis Bacon painted hanging meat as an image of mortality and suffering. Shahabuddin works in a similar expressive tradition, and the drips and raw pinks here support that reading. Thirst then becomes desire or deprivation in a broader sense: the body's hunger for life. At Tk 50 lakh, it is by far the most expensive work in the room. It is also the most naked about need.
Monirul Islam, Let There Be Light, oil and acrylic on canvas, 36 x 42 inches

Monirul Islam goes further. Let There Be Light (2017) is built on newspaper, and beneath the grey paint we can still read the clippings. The title is the oldest command in Genesis, the first words spoken over the dark. It also appears in the work as the headline of one of those clippings, an article by Ananta Yusuf, my colleague at The Daily Star, written two years after the Rana Plaza disaster. Beside it runs another headline: "Two years of denial and betrayal." The 2013 collapse of a garment factory outside Dhaka killed more than 1,100 workers. A slumped grey figure sits on the clipping. Around it, the white canvas is scattered with crayon marks in green and yellow, as if ordinary life were still going on at the edges of the page. The scriptural phrase, set over a story of buried workers, reads like an unanswered prayer.
Mohammad Eunus, Evidence, Mixed media on canvas, 36 x 36 inches

Not every painting lets you in. I will admit that Mohammad Eunus’s Evidence defeated me. I stood in front of it longer than almost anything else in the room and came away with more questions than answers. Strips of frayed cloth or paper are laid across the canvas like bricks, then buried under paint that has been poured, scraped and left to blister. A rust-coloured stain spreads across the middle, and scraps of handwriting surface here and there, like graffiti half erased by rain. The nearest I came to it was the feeling of standing before an old wall in Old Dhaka, sensing years of weather and lives pressed into its surface without knowing a single one of their stories. Perhaps that is the point. The title promises evidence, but it does not say of what. His abstraction is deeply rooted in the urban textures, chaos, and historical decay of Bangladesh's landscapes. Perhaps that is why Eunus leaves us standing there: not to decode the surface, but simply to feel what time has done to it.

His Wild was easier to hold on to. It is a torn scrap of corrugated cardboard, the ridges laid bare. Eunus has framed this piece of packing box behind glass, on a dark ground, the way a museum might display a fragment of an ancient manuscript. A thing made to be thrown away becomes something to look at slowly. Seen beside Evidence, it suggests that the humblest materials of daily life, a box, a rag, a wall, keep their own record, and that an artist’s job may simply be to frame it.

Ranjit Das is far more direct. Man and his Environment is a triangular canvas, red with white bands, shaped like a road sign. At its centre is a man's face, cracked like dry earth, and below it a small gold lock. Shahid Kazi's A Fallen Sunflower, painted on the scale of a fallen body, shows a single bloom collapsing on its broken stem. And in Shahid Kabir's Lost in Sea, one wooden boat drifts on a churning grey-green sea, with no shore in sight.

What holds people up when the ground shifts? Again and again, the show’s answer is the same: family.

Sheikh Afzal Hossain paints them as if they were weathered frescoes, figures etched in grey and white over scraped, dusty grounds. In Family, a father carries a small boy on his shoulders while the mother holds a baby close beside him, the whole group pressed together as if against a wind. In Mother & Child, a young mother cradles an infant while an older child stands a little apart. The adults in both paintings look down, weighed by something we are not shown. But in each, one child lifts its eyes and looks straight at us. It is the most quietly insistent gaze in the room, and it makes the viewer part of the family’s burden.

Jamal Ahmed offers the opposite view, and a surprise. The painter of the charging bulls turns out to be capable of great gentleness. In a small untitled work on paper, a woman in a white sari with a red border walks toward the sea, holding hands with three children, while a lone figure stands in a fishing boat on the horizon. Where Afzal’s children face us, Jamal’s family walks away, and we never see their faces. Perhaps they are going to meet the boat; the painting will not say. The dust he kicked up for the bulls has become sea mist here, and the force of his brush has softened into tenderness.

Then comes the land itself. Ahmed Shamsuddoha’s A Day of Cowboys is the most photographic painting on view: cowherd boys and grazing cattle in a sunlit meadow under a monsoon cloud the colour of slate. Look to the far right, past the herds, and pale city buildings are rising above the trees. Hashem Khan, one of the country's most senior painters, returns to the village he has painted for decades, with a woman carrying an armful of water lilies in the dusk-blue Girl.

Abdus Shakoor Shah, long devoted to folk ballads, builds his canvas on an old song, like a page from an illustrated manuscript: flat, black-outlined panels of lime green, violet and orange, dotted and striped, lined with rows of black clay pots. At the top, three women gather, two in profile turned toward the third, who looks straight out. Below them, a man with a tilak on his forehead gazes solemnly back. Between them, in a band of orange, Shakoor has written out a passage of Bangla verse in which a matchmaker arrives at a family’s door, praises the daughter’s beauty and urges a marriage now that she has come of age. It is a scene repeated for generations and now preserved here in the rhythm of an old song, as if the painter wanted to keep not only the story but the way it was once told.
Farida Zaman, Sufia, acrylic on paper, 47 x 47 inches

Shakoor’s bride is discussed and praised, but never named. Farida Zaman gives hers a name. Her Sufia is a long-necked woman with dark, wavy hair, painted in the flat, rhythmic style of Bengali folk art, her gaze calm and a little heavy-lidded. She clasps a pale, half-transparent figure to her chest, and sits behind a great oval of catch, a basket or a boat holding an enormous fish patterned with red and yellow zigzags. Above her, veils of yellow light and fine white lines spread across a deep blue ground like a net cast over water. Where Shakoor’s woman belongs to a song, Sufia belongs to the river, and to herself.

These paintings do not mourn the past. They hold on to it, piece by bright piece: water lilies in the dusk and a red-bordered sari.
Jahangir Hossain, Waiting, acrylic on canvas, 52 x 36 inches

Somewhere in the middle of the show, the mood lifts. Someone has to turn toward the light. In Jahangir Hossain's Waiting, a young woman stands with her back half to us, her hair tied with a red band, her face turned toward a burst of gold that could be a doorway or a window. We never see her eyes. Do we need to? Her body is a dark silhouette, but wherever the light touches it, her blouse and sari flare into red, yellow and green, as if the brightness were warming her skin. It is the most sensual painting in the room, and the most private. Who is she waiting for? The painter is silent. 
Hashem Khan, Bok, acrylic on canvas, 24 x 30 inches

Birds are everywhere. In Hashem Khan's Bok, egrets crowd a field of ultramarine beneath a band of hot yellow, their necks craning upward. In Rafiqun Nabi’s 1997 watercolour Bird, a spotted ochre bird flies in front of a tall, turreted tower painted in the same colour, so that bird and tower almost merge; below them, a larger crested grey bird stands on red legs, and the three come together like a strange totem on a pale shore that could be a beach, a riverbank or the edge of a village pond. 
Kanak Chanpa Chakma, The Bell, acrylic on canvas, 30 x 42 inches

Kanak Chanpa Chakma, whose work has long drawn on the life of the Chakma people of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, gives the show its sound. In The Bell, a heavy blue-black bell tilts mid-swing against a sky split between blazing red above and scraped yellow below, a knotted red cord trailing from it. Light strikes its shoulder in a burst of gold, as if the moment of ringing had been caught. Her Ritual is the same idea in a whisper. Three dark, gourd-shaped vessels with green stoppers stand together under a deep, grainy blue, and off to one side, alone, sits a small red pot holding a few red flowers. No people appear, yet the canvas feels arranged for a rite about to begin. One painting calls out, the other waits in silence for what the call will bring.
Rafiqun Nabi, Bird, watercolour on paper, 22 x 30 inches

Gulshan Hossain’s Silence Within takes that silence and sets it inside a fire. Almost the entire canvas is a deep, saturated red, broken at the edges by blotted patches of black and silver that look like scorched or weathered walls. Only in the lower corner does anything take recognisable shape: a single pale hibiscus, the joba of every Bengali courtyard, painted with a delicacy found nowhere else on the surface. Against all that heat, it does not wilt. It is the stillness the title promises, small and stubborn, and it had sold by the time I reached it.

Two painters let go of images altogether. Rokeya Sultana, a senior printmaker, works here in tempera. Flaming Desires is a glowing core of crimson and hot pink, as if lit from behind; at its edges, the paint breaks into speckles and cracked crusts, and at the top a drift of white, blue and acid green cools the heat like smoke. Maksuda Iqbal Nipa’s Radiant Colours is calmer but no less hot: a band of crimson melting into blazing yellow and orange, under a thin line of violet, its surface crinkled like bark so that the light catches on thousands of tiny ridges. Neither painting depicts anything. Both ask simply to be felt, the way you feel the sun on your face before you open your eyes.

Walk the show the way I did, and it closes on two images of love, one in feathers, one in faces.

Hasura Akter Rumky’s Harmony’s Dance unfolds across two slender canvases, placed side by side, like a pair of open doors. In each, two white doves meet in mid-air, wings spread, beaks touching, one pair against gold and the other against rust. The dove is the plainest symbol in the room, and it carries two meanings at once. It is the old sign of peace. It is also a sign of devotion, a bird long associated with faithful pairs and with lovers. Rumky paints both meanings into one gesture: the kiss of beaks is an act of tenderness, and also a truce. Her doves are not escaping anything. They hover, wings fully open, at the exact point where two bodies stop moving apart. 

The backgrounds matter too. The textured gold of one panel and the deep rust of the other read like dawn and dusk, or like old gilded walls, so the birds seem to hang between times.

Across the gallery hangs Anisuzzaman Anis's Love Conquers All, a controlled and decorative piece in a good sense, but it doesn’t take the emotional risks that some of the rawer work in the show does. Anisuzzaman is a printmaker and a professor at the University of Dhaka, best known for decades of woodcuts about the city's stacked concrete. Here he turns that structural mind on people. Faces overlap without hiding one another, and that’s the whole idea made visible: people sharing space without erasing each other. Soft coral and salmon faces float against a smoky, plum-grey ground that darkens almost to black, and at the centre, where the profiles overlap most, the pinks flare into bright red, like a pulse showing through skin. It is love painted without sugar.

In a social media statement on the series, Anisuzzaman presents it as a reply to "the global climate of conflict and hatred," and the faces show what he means. They have no individual features; no one's faith, class or nation can be read from them. They share space, even share outlines, and none of them disappears. The title Anisuzzaman chose is 2,000 years old. Omnia vincit amor comes from Virgil. 

Standing between the doves and the faces, with the bulls still charging somewhere behind us, the Roman poet’s words stop sounding like a greetings-card sentiment.

Arun Devnath is the Deputy Editor at The Daily Star.
