It also appears in the work as the headline of one of those clippings, an article by Ananta Yusuf, my colleague at The Daily Star, written two years after the Rana Plaza disaster. Beside it runs another headline: "Two years of denial and betrayal." The 2013 collapse of a garment factory outside Dhaka killed more than 1,100 workers. A slumped grey figure sits on the clipping. Around it, the white canvas is scattered with crayon marks in green and yellow, as if ordinary life were still going on at the edges of the page. The scriptural phrase, set over a story of buried workers, reads like an unanswered prayer.
Mohammad Eunus, Evidence, Mixed media on canvas, 36 x 36 inches

Not every painting lets you in. I will admit that Mohammad Eunus’s Evidence defeated me. I stood in front of it longer than almost anything else in the room and came away with more questions than answers. Strips of frayed cloth or paper are laid across the canvas like bricks, then buried under paint that has been poured, scraped and left to blister. A rust-coloured stain spreads across the middle, and scraps of handwriting surface here and there, like graffiti half erased by rain. The nearest I came to it was the feeling of standing before an old wall in Old Dhaka, sensing years of weather and lives pressed into its surface without knowing a single one of their stories. Perhaps that is the point. The title promises evidence, but it does not say of what. His abstraction is deeply rooted in the urban textures, chaos, and historical decay of Bangladesh's landscapes. Perhaps that is why Eunus leaves us standing there: not to decode the surface, but simply to feel what time has done to it.

His Wild was easier to hold on to. It is a torn scrap of corrugated cardboard, the ridges laid bare. Eunus has framed this piece of packing box behind glass, on a dark ground, the way a museum might display a fragment of an ancient manuscript. A thing made to be thrown away becomes something to look at slowly. Seen beside Evidence, it suggests that the humblest materials of daily life, a box, a rag, a wall, keep their own record, and that an artist’s job may simply be to frame it.

Ranjit Das is far more direct. Man and his Environment is a triangular canvas, red with white bands, shaped like a road sign. At its centre is a man's face, cracked like dry earth, and below it a small gold lock. Shahid Kazi's A Fallen Sunflower, painted on the scale of a fallen body, shows a single bloom collapsing on its broken stem. And in Shahid Kabir's Lost in Sea, one wooden boat drifts on a churning grey-green sea, with no shore in sight.

What holds people up when the ground shifts? Again and again, the show’s answer is the same: family.

Sheikh Afzal Hossain paints them as if they were weathered frescoes, figures etched in grey and white over scraped, dusty grounds. In Family, a father carries a small boy on his shoulders while the mother holds a baby close beside him, the whole group pressed together as if against a wind. In Mother & Child, a young mother cradles an infant while an older child stands a little apart. The adults in both paintings look down, weighed by something we are not shown. But in each, one child lifts its eyes and looks straight at us. It is the most quietly insistent gaze in the room, and it makes the viewer part of the family’s burden.

Jamal Ahmed offers the opposite view, and a surprise. The painter of the charging bulls turns out to be capable of great gentleness. In a small untitled work on paper, a woman in a white sari with a red border walks toward the sea, holding hands with three children, while a lone figure stands in a fishing boat on the horizon. Where Afzal’s children face us, Jamal’s family walks away, and we never see their faces. Perhaps they are going to meet the boat; the painting will not say. The dust he kicked up for the bulls has become sea mist here, and the force of his brush has softened into tenderness.

Then comes the land itself. Ahmed Shamsuddoha’s A Day of Cowboys is the most photographic painting on view: cowherd boys and grazing cattle in a sunlit meadow under a monsoon cloud the colour of slate. Look to the far right, past the herds, and pale city buildings are rising above the trees. Hashem Khan, one of the country's most senior painters, returns to the village he has painted for decades, with a woman carrying an armful of water lilies in the dusk-blue Girl.

Abdus Shakoor Shah, long devoted to folk ballads, builds his canvas on an old song, like a page from an illustrated manuscript: flat, black-outlined panels of lime green, violet and orange, dotted and striped, lined with rows of black clay pots. At the top, three women gather, two in profile turned toward the third, who looks straight out. Below them, a man with a tilak on his forehead gazes solemnly back. Between them, in a band of orange, Shakoor has written out a passage of Bangla verse in which a matchmaker arrives at a family’s door, praises the daughter’s beauty and urges a marriage now that she has come of age. It is a scene repeated for generations and now preserved here in the rhythm of an old song, as if the painter wanted to keep not only the story but the way it was once told.
Farida Zaman, Sufia, acrylic on paper, 47 x 47 inches

Shakoor’s bride is discussed and praised, but never named. Farida Zaman gives hers a name. Her Sufia is a long-necked woman with dark, wavy hair, painted in the flat, rhythmic style of Bengali folk art, her gaze calm and a little heavy-lidded. She clasps a pale, half-transparent figure to her chest, and sits behind a great oval of catch, a basket or a boat holding an enormous fish patterned with red and yellow zigzags. Above her, veils of yellow light and fine white lines spread across a deep blue ground like a net cast over water. Where Shakoor’s woman belongs to a song, Sufia belongs to the river, and to herself.

These paintings do not mourn the past. They hold on to it, piece by bright piece: water lilies in the dusk and a red-bordered sari.
Jahangir Hossain, Waiting, acrylic on canvas, 52 x 36 inches

Somewhere in the middle of the show, the mood lifts. Someone has to turn toward the light. In Jahangir Hossain's Waiting, a young woman stands with her back half to us, her hair tied with a red band, her face turned toward a burst of gold that could be a doorway or a window. We never see her eyes. Do we need to? Her body is a dark silhouette, but wherever the light touches it, her blouse and sari flare into red, yellow and green, as if the brightness were warming her skin. It is the most sensual painting in the room, and the most private. Who is she waiting for? The painter is silent. 
Hashem Khan, Bok, acrylic on canvas, 24 x 30 inches

Birds are everywhere. In Hashem Khan's Bok, egrets crowd a field of ultramarine beneath a band of hot yellow, their necks craning upward. In Rafiqun Nabi’s 1997 watercolour Bird, a spotted ochre bird flies in front of a tall, turreted tower painted in the same colour, so that bird and tower almost merge; below them, a larger crested grey bird stands on red legs, and the three come together like a strange totem on a pale shore that could be a beach, a riverbank or the edge of a village pond. 
Kanak Chanpa Chakma, The Bell, acrylic on canvas, 30 x 42 inches

Kanak Chanpa Chakma, whose work has long drawn on the life of the Chakma people of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, gives the show its sound. In The Bell, a heavy blue-black bell tilts mid-swing against a sky split between blazing red above and scraped yellow below, a knotted red cord trailing from it. Light strikes its shoulder in a burst of gold, as if the moment of ringing had been caught. Her Ritual is the same idea in a whisper. Three dark, gourd-shaped vessels with green stoppers stand together under a deep, grainy blue, and off to one side, alone, sits a small red pot holding a few red flowers. No people appear, yet the canvas feels arranged for a rite about to begin. One painting calls out, the other waits in silence for what the call will bring.
Rafiqun Nabi, Bird, watercolour on paper, 22 x 30 inches

Gulshan Hossain’s Silence Within takes that silence and sets it inside a fire. Almost the entire canvas is a deep, saturated red, broken at the edges by blotted patches of black and silver that look like scorched or weathered walls. Only in the lower corner does anything take recognisable shape: a single pale hibiscus, the joba of every Bengali courtyard, painted with a delicacy found nowhere else on the surface. Against all that heat, it does not wilt. It is the stillness the title promises, small and stubborn, and it had sold by the time I reached it.

Two painters let go of images altogether. Rokeya Sultana, a senior printmaker, works here in tempera. Flaming Desires is a glowing core of crimson and hot pink, as if lit from behind; at its edges, the paint breaks into speckles and cracked crusts, and at the top a drift of white, blue and acid green cools the heat like smoke. Maksuda Iqbal Nipa’s Radiant Colours is calmer but no less hot: a band of crimson melting into blazing yellow and orange, under a thin line of violet, its surface crinkled like bark so that the light catches on thousands of tiny ridges. Neither painting depicts anything. Both ask simply to be felt, the way you feel the sun on your face before you open your eyes.

Walk the show the way I did, and it closes on two images of love, one in feathers, one in faces.

Hasura Akter Rumky’s Harmony’s Dance unfolds across two slender canvases, placed side by side, like a pair of open doors. In each, two white doves meet in mid-air, wings spread, beaks touching, one pair against gold and the other against rust. The dove is the plainest symbol in the room, and it carries two meanings at once. It is the old sign of peace. It is also a sign of devotion, a bird long associated with faithful pairs and with lovers. Rumky paints both meanings into one gesture: the kiss of beaks is an act of tenderness, and also a truce. Her doves are not escaping anything. They hover, wings fully open, at the exact point where two bodies stop moving apart. 

The backgrounds matter too. The textured gold of one panel and the deep rust of the other read like dawn and dusk, or like old gilded walls, so the birds seem to hang between times.

Across the gallery hangs Anisuzzaman Anis's Love Conquers All, a controlled and decorative piece in a good sense, but it doesn’t take the emotional risks that some of the rawer work in the show does. Anisuzzaman is a printmaker and a professor at the University of Dhaka, best known for decades of woodcuts about the city's stacked concrete. Here he turns that structural mind on people. Faces overlap without hiding one another, and that’s the whole idea made visible: people sharing space without erasing each other. Soft coral and salmon faces float against a smoky, plum-grey ground that darkens almost to black, and at the centre, where the profiles overlap most, the pinks flare into bright red, like a pulse showing through skin. It is love painted without sugar.

In a social media statement on the series, Anisuzzaman presents it as a reply to "the global climate of conflict and hatred," and the faces show what he means. They have no individual features; no one's faith, class or nation can be read from them. They share space, even share outlines, and none of them disappears. The title Anisuzzaman chose is 2,000 years old. Omnia vincit amor comes from Virgil. 

Standing between the doves and the faces, with the bulls still charging somewhere behind us, the Roman poet’s words stop sounding like a greetings-card sentiment.

Arun Devnath is the Deputy Editor at The Daily Star.

item.title: The Daily Star – Can Bangladesh create ten million jobs in five years?
item.description:
Imagine a train that gets faster with every passing year, yet takes on fewer passengers at each station. On paper, the railway is a success. For the crowds left waiting on the platforms, it is not. Bangladesh’s economy faces a similar conundrum, as years of strong growth have not translated into a commensurate expansion of employment. Economists call this jobless growth. In principle, as an economy produces more goods and services, firms need more workers to meet rising demand. But when growth relies increasingly on machinery, technology and other forms of capital rather than additional labour, output can expand without a corresponding increase in employment.

For much of the past decade, Bangladesh’s economy grew by around 6.5 per cent a year. Yet aggregate growth figures obscure a more complicated picture. Agriculture’s share of GDP has declined over time, while industry and services have gained ground. Employment, however, has not shifted in the same way. According to the Labour Force Survey 2024, agriculture accounted for around 45 per cent of employed people, compared with 17 per cent in industry and 38 per cent in services, yet it contributed only about 11 per cent of GDP that year. A large share of the workforce therefore remains in a sector that generates a relatively small share of national output. Moving workers into more productive activities, while creating enough jobs for the roughly two million people who enter the labour market each year, is a major policy challenge.
Candidates wait outside an examination centre ahead of a government recruitment test in July 2025. The shortage of formal employment opportunities has intensified competition for government jobs, particularly among educated young people. Photo: Prabir Das

The government’s Five-Year Strategic Framework (FYSF) sets a target of creating ten million jobs over five years and identifies employment generation as its “top priority”. Can Bangladesh meet this target under its current pattern of growth? This essay draws on two papers I co-authored with Dr Syed Abul Basher, which trace how employment has responded to output growth since the early 2000s. Our analysis suggests that meeting the target will be difficult without changes to the way growth generates jobs.

A simple measure of a complicated problem

It helps first to clarify one idea that economists lean on heavily: employment elasticity. Imagine a shop whose sales grow by 10 per cent in a year. If the owner takes on 5 per cent more staff, the shop’s employment elasticity is 0.5. If sales grow just as fast but the owner buys a card machine and a barcode scanner instead, and no extra staff are needed, the elasticity is close to zero. The shop has grown, but it has not created any work.

Apply that idea to the whole economy (Figure 1). Around 2010, every one per cent of growth brought roughly half a per cent more employment. By the mid-2010s, it brought less than a fifth of a per cent. The 2022 survey showed a partial recovery, but for an uncomfortable reason: when the pandemic shut workplaces and sent migrant workers home, many people fell back on the family farm. Over longer periods, which smooth out such shocks, growth since 2013 has generated much less employment than it did before.
Figure 1: Employment elasticity: the % rise in employment for every 1% of GDP growth. Source: Basher and Salim (2026)

Manufacturing grows, its workforce does not

The place to start is manufacturing. In the classic path to prosperity, the one South Korea, Taiwan and later China followed, factories draw people out of low-paid farm work into steadier, better-paid jobs. For two decades, Bangladesh’s garment industry did exactly that.

That role has now reversed. By our estimates, manufacturing was the largest single source of employment growth up to 2013. Since then, its output has kept growing faster than the rest of the economy while its workforce has shrunk, so it now pulls job creation down rather than up (Figure 2). Manufacturing employment fell from about 9.5 million in 2013 to about 8.1 million in 2024, even as garment exports more than tripled between 2010 and 2023 and garment employment stayed at roughly four million.
Figure 2: Each sector’s contribution to the economy-wide employment elasticity. Source: Basher and Salim (2026)

This aggregate decline conceals a sharp difference between men and women. The number of men employed in manufacturing rose slightly over the decade. The number of women fell from about 3.8 million in 2013 to just under 2 million in 2024, and women’s share of manufacturing employment fell from 40 per cent to 24 per cent (Figure 3). The net loss of manufacturing employment has been almost entirely a loss of women’s employment.
Figure 3: People employed in manufacturing, in millions. Source: BBS Labour Force Surveys

Where women’s employment has grown instead is on the farm: three in four employed women now work in agriculture. Women’s employment has long been far more responsive to growth than men’s, but much of the increase has come in agriculture, even when farm output grew only modestly. This trend has been described as the “feminisation of agriculture”. The ladder that carried a generation of women from the village to the factory floor is being quietly pulled up.

Three forces behind the change

Why has growth become less job-rich, and why have women borne the brunt? The evidence points to three forces. They probably reinforce one another, and the data cannot tell us precisely how much each one matters.

The first is capital deepening: firms have been investing more in machinery and equipment relative to the number of people they employ. Between 2001 and 2019, adding capital for each hour of work contributed considerably more to productivity growth than improvements in technology and efficiency did. Capital accumulation accelerated in the mid-2010s, when the link between growth and employment was particularly weak. The coincidence is suggestive, but it is not proof of causation.

The second is a change in the structure of manufacturing, particularly in garments. Greater automation and the closure of smaller firms may help explain why manufacturing employment fell even as output and exports grew, with the pandemic adding to the pressure. This is not a story of robots sweeping through the economy: most Bangladeshi manufacturers remain far from the technological frontier, and most firms that adopted new machines or software kept the same number of workers. The decline appears to reflect capital-intensive investment more than the replacement of workers by technology. Women have been more exposed. The small garment enterprises that closed after 2012 relied heavily on low-skilled female workers, and their decline weakened job creation for young urban women. Where new machines have changed tasks, the effect has fallen on entry-level helper and assistant-operator positions, in which women are concentrated. 

The third is the pattern of growth itself. The sectors driving growth are not the ones that employ most people. Agriculture employs close to half the workforce but has grown more slowly than the economy as a whole in every period we studied. Finance and public administration have expanded quickly, yet each employs less than 2 per cent of workers. Manufacturing came closest to combining fast growth with large-scale employment in 2010–2017, but has since shifted towards much weaker job creation.
Day labourers wait along a road in Mirpur, Dhaka, hoping to find work. With 84 per cent of Bangladesh’s workforce engaged in informal employment, many workers face irregular earnings, low wages and job insecurity. Photo: Prabir Das

Work moves to less productive sectors

The economy has not stopped generating work, but the work is increasingly found where productivity is lower and conditions are weaker. Construction, shops, transport, and hotels and restaurants have continued adding workers throughout, and in recent years they have accounted for most of the economy’s employment growth. Remittance-financed spending on houses, shops and local services has helped sustain demand in these sectors, though this says little about the quality of the work.

On quality, the picture is less encouraging. Much of this work is self-employment: a tea stall, a battery-run van, a small repair shop. In 2024, more people in Bangladesh worked on their own account than for an employer, and 84 per cent of workers were in informal employment, rising to more than nine in ten among employed women. Such work is mostly small-scale, insecure and poorly paid.

Young, educated and waiting

For young people entering the labour market, these shifts mean narrowing choices. The factory route has shrunk, especially for young women; much of the remaining work is informal and low-paid; and formal jobs for the educated have not grown fast enough to absorb them. University graduates now have the highest unemployment rate of any education group. A degree that once led to a desk now often leads to a long wait.

Young women face the steepest odds. Among women in their late twenties, almost a third are neither in work nor in education or training (Figure 4). Whatever the role of household responsibilities, the decline of small garment enterprises has removed one of the few routes into paid employment that young women once had.
Figure 4: Share of young people neither in employment nor in education or training (NEET), 2024. Source: BBS Labour Force Survey 2024.

These pressures help explain why secure, formal employment has become so politically charged. The 2024 student movement began as a protest against quotas in public-sector recruitment before growing into something much larger. Labour-market frustration was not the only cause, but it was part of the backdrop.

The arithmetic of ten million

The FYSF, to its credit, shows its working. It projects employment in each sector by multiplying expected growth by an assumed employment elasticity, based on patterns it describes as having been observed between 2010 and 2017. With growth rising to 8.5 per cent, it arrives at about 9.8 million additional people in work at home; the remaining half a million or so comes from a projected rise in workers going abroad each year.

The difficulty is that these assumptions reflect a more job-rich period. They imply that employment will respond to growth far more strongly than it has, on average, since 2010, and that manufacturing will again become a major source of employment, although its elasticity has been close to zero or negative for most of the past decade.

Figure 5 shows how much this matters. We keep the framework’s growth path, starting point and projection for overseas employment, and change only how strongly employment at home responds to growth. If manufacturing employment behaves as it did between 2010 and 2022, total additional employment comes to about 8.4 million rather than 10.2 million. If the whole economy behaves as it did in that period, it falls to about 6.2 million. If growth also averages 5.5 per cent, it falls to about 4.6 million.
Additional employment between FY2026 and FY2031 under different assumptions in millions. Source: Basher and Salim (2026)

These are scenarios, not forecasts, and a different policy environment could produce a different result. They show that if employment keeps responding to growth as it has in recent years, faster growth alone is unlikely to be enough. The timing adds urgency: when Bangladesh loses its least-developed-country trade preferences in Europe in 2029, around 14 per cent of exports will face new tariff costs, mostly on garments.

Making growth work for employment

What would it take to make growth and employment go hand in hand? We see three broad reform objectives.

The first is to make industrial growth more employment-intensive. The FYSF already gives priority to agro-processing, leather and pharmaceuticals, alongside ICT. These industries, together with light engineering, share the garment industry’s labour-intensive character and have substantial export potential. Remittance-financed demand for household durables such as refrigerators, largely met by domestic manufacturers, shows that the home market can also support industrial employment. Since the recent fall in manufacturing employment appears to reflect capital-intensive investment, support for these industries should favour firms that grow while employing large numbers of people. With trade preferences set to shrink, broadening the export base is no longer optional.

The second is to widen access to productive work, starting with women. Women’s employment has responded strongly to growth in the sectors that employ them, as it did when the garment industry expanded. Partial automation reduces repetitive tasks but raises demand for complementary skills such as machine operation and quality control, the very skills the FYSF lists as the garment industry’s main gaps. The framework’s plan to retrain 10,000 female workers in its first year is a start. Scaled up and aimed at women already on factory floors, such training would let modernisation and women’s employment advance together.

The same objective calls for looking beyond factories. Construction, logistics, healthcare and selected traditional services combine growth potential with the capacity to absorb workers. Health stands out: its output has recently outpaced the economy, which may point to rising post-pandemic demand for care. Bangladesh has less than a quarter of the doctors, nurses and midwives per person that the World Health Organization recommends, so the FYSF’s pledge to recruit 100,000 health workers is welcome. Educated young people need better-quality education and skills training for expanding service sectors, and the FYSF’s planned apprenticeships and first-job employment subsidies point in the right direction. Since much new work comes from small enterprises and self-employment, regulatory reforms and workforce development could make it more secure and better paid; the FYSF’s planned credit for small agro-enterprises, including a women-targeted line, could help.
Garment workers walk to their factories along the Dhaka–Aricha Highway in Ullail, Savar. Despite rising production and exports, manufacturing employment has declined, with women accounting for almost the entire net loss of jobs since 2013. Photo: Palash Khan

The third is to align public policy with employment outcomes. That means monitoring closely and correcting course to help workers move from agriculture into sectors absorbing more labour, such as construction, transport, and hotels and restaurants. It requires timely labour data, and the FYSF’s planned real-time labour market information system is a good place to start. Because assumed employment elasticities largely determine how many jobs a growth target appears to deliver, they should be updated whenever new survey data arrive. The FYSF itself states that its parameters are open to revision; the next Labour Force Survey is the natural moment to revise them.

Faster, and fuller

Bangladesh’s growth story has never been only about GDP. It mattered because it brought millions of people, many of them women, into paid work for the first time. Over the past decade, that link has weakened. Manufacturing keeps growing but no longer adds workers; employment has shifted towards farming and informal services; and a large, educated generation of young people is left waiting.

None of this is cause for despair. Bangladesh has confounded pessimists before, and the new government is right to put employment first. To return to the train with which we began: the answer is not to slow it down, but to make sure more people can board. The real test of the next five years will not be how fast the economy grows, but how many people find productive work as it does.

Asaf Ibne Salim is a senior research associate at Research and Policy Integration for Development (RAPID), Dhaka.

Remittance-financed spending on houses, shops and local services has helped sustain demand in these sectors, though this says little about the quality of the work.

On quality, the picture is less encouraging. Much of this work is self-employment: a tea stall, a battery-run van, a small repair shop. In 2024, more people in Bangladesh worked on their own account than for an employer, and 84 per cent of workers were in informal employment, rising to more than nine in ten among employed women. Such work is mostly small-scale, insecure and poorly paid.

Young, educated and waiting

For young people entering the labour market, these shifts mean narrowing choices. The factory route has shrunk, especially for young women; much of the remaining work is informal and low-paid; and formal jobs for the educated have not grown fast enough to absorb them. University graduates now have the highest unemployment rate of any education group. A degree that once led to a desk now often leads to a long wait.

Young women face the steepest odds. Among women in their late twenties, almost a third are neither in work nor in education or training (Figure 4). Whatever the role of household responsibilities, the decline of small garment enterprises has removed one of the few routes into paid employment that young women once had.

These pressures help explain why secure, formal employment has become so politically charged. The 2024 student movement began as a protest against quotas in public-sector recruitment before growing into something much larger. Labour-market frustration was not the only cause, but it was part of the backdrop.

The arithmetic of ten million

The FYSF, to its credit, shows its working. It projects employment in each sector by multiplying expected growth by an assumed employment elasticity, based on patterns it describes as having been observed between 2010 and 2017. With growth rising to 8.5 per cent, it arrives at about 9.8 million additional people in work at home; the remaining half a million or so comes from a projected rise in workers going abroad each year.

The difficulty is that these assumptions reflect a more job-rich period. They imply that employment will respond to growth far more strongly than it has, on average, since 2010, and that manufacturing will again become a major source of employment, although its elasticity has been close to zero or negative for most of the past decade.

These are scenarios, not forecasts, and a different policy environment could produce a different result. They show that if employment keeps responding to growth as it has in recent years, faster growth alone is unlikely to be enough. The timing adds urgency: when Bangladesh loses its least-developed-country trade preferences in Europe in 2029, around 14 per cent of exports will face new tariff costs, mostly on garments.

Making growth work for employment

What would it take to make growth and employment go hand in hand? We see three broad reform objectives.

The first is to make industrial growth more employment-intensive. The FYSF already gives priority to agro-processing, leather and pharmaceuticals, alongside ICT. The second is to widen access to productive work, starting with women. The same objective calls for looking beyond factories. Construction, logistics, healthcare and selected traditional services combine growth potential with the capacity to absorb workers. Health stands out: its output has recently outpaced the economy, which may point to rising post-pandemic demand for care. Bangladesh has less than a quarter of the doctors, nurses and midwives per person that the World Health Organization recommends, so the FYSF’s pledge to recruit 100,000 health workers is welcome. Educated young people need better-quality education and skills training for expanding service sectors, and the FYSF’s planned apprenticeships and first-job employment subsidies point in the right direction. Since much new work comes from small enterprises and self-employment, regulatory reforms and workforce development could make it more secure and better paid; the FYSF’s planned credit for small agro-enterprises, including a women-targeted line, could help.
Garment workers walk to their factories along the Dhaka–Aricha Highway in Ullail, Savar. Despite rising production and exports, manufacturing employment has declined, with women accounting for almost the entire net loss of jobs since 2013. Photo: Palash Khan

The third is to align public policy with employment outcomes. That means monitoring closely and correcting course to help workers move from agriculture into sectors absorbing more labour, such as construction, transport, and hotels and restaurants. It requires timely labour data, and the FYSF’s planned real-time labour market information system is a good place to start. Because assumed employment elasticities largely determine how many jobs a growth target appears to deliver, they should be updated whenever new survey data arrive. The FYSF itself states that its parameters are open to revision; the next Labour Force Survey is the natural moment to revise them.

Faster, and fuller

Bangladesh’s growth story has never been only about GDP. It mattered because it brought millions of people, many of them women, into paid work for the first time. Over the past decade, that link has weakened. Manufacturing keeps growing but no longer adds workers; employment has shifted towards farming and informal services; and a large, educated generation of young people is left waiting.

None of this is cause for despair. Bangladesh has confounded pessimists before, and the new government is right to put employment first. To return to the train with which we began: the answer is not to slow it down, but to make sure more people can board. The real test of the next five years will not be how fast the economy grows, but how many people find productive work as it does.

item.title: The Daily Star – Can Bangladesh fix its battery rickshaw problem after two decades of neglect?
item.description:
On 2 November 2026, registration of battery-powered rickshaws began in thirteen city corporations across Bangladesh, nearly two decades after the vehicles first appeared on the country's roads. In Dhaka South, the authorities began selling application forms for Tk 100 each, with approvals to be issued in batches of several hundred or several thousand. Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: how many battery-powered rickshaws should ultimately be allowed to operate in these cities? After two decades of largely unregulated expansion, the government has finally begun registering the vehicles without first establishing a clear limit on their numbers.

The scale of the problem becomes clear when we consider a basic question: how many battery-powered rickshaws are operating on Bangladesh's roads? The government has no reliable figure. In September 2026, the home minister told parliament that the number stood at between fifty and eighty lakh, or five to eight million. The difference between the lower and upper estimates is three million vehicles, highlighting the extent of the uncertainty. Such a wide gap raises serious questions about the government's ability to monitor and regulate the sector. Over the years, inadequate oversight has allowed the number of battery-powered rickshaws to grow unchecked, creating a transport system that operates largely outside an effective regulatory framework.

A business, not a plan

The usual story is that the government, in a burst of green enthusiasm, put battery rickshaws on the road and then lost control. The record, however, tells a different story. The vehicles entered the market through commercial initiatives, with government agencies that stood to benefit financially facilitating their introduction, while the authority responsible for regulating them failed to exercise effective oversight. The clearest primary account comes from news reporting in May 2011, when the first ban was already being drafted. It records that Maa Enterprise first introduced the vehicles commercially in Cumilla in 2004 and then joined forces with Bangladesh Diesel Plant to import three-wheelers from China and market them from 2008. 
Battery-powered rickshaws being charged at a garage near Dhaka airport, where at least 40 vehicles are charged daily for Tk 80–100 each. Unregulated charging facilities and illegal electricity connections have added to the economic costs of the sector's rapid expansion. Photo: Anisur Rahman

When consulted, the Dhaka Transport Coordination Board (now the Dhaka Transport Coordination Authority, or DTCA) said the rickshaws would reduce fuel consumption and environmental pollution. The Bangladesh Road Transport Authority told importers the vehicles were non-motorised and that local government could decide their fate. And Dhaka City Corporation, in 2009, approved 7,000 of them and collected a licence fee of 1,500 taka each, but never issued the licences because the ministry never approved a policy under which to issue them.

So a state body took money from thousands of vehicle owners before any rule existed to govern the vehicle. The fee was real; the licence was fiction. This marked the beginning of Bangladesh's battery rickshaw problem, driven not by accident but by the pursuit of revenue. What no one supplied, at any stage, was a design. A battery rickshaw, as it actually exists, is a pedal rickshaw frame with a motor and a stack of lead-acid batteries bolted on. It was never engineered to carry that weight at that speed. Professor Md Ehsan of BUET, whose team spent years developing a safe standard, made the engineer's point plainly: a frame built for a man pedalling cannot safely be ridden at thirty kilometres an hour. The home minister who announced a ban in 2021 put the same fact in blunter terms, noting that only the front wheel had brakes. The country motorised a vehicle without first deciding what the vehicle should be.

Bans that did not hold

Once the fleet was out, the state fell into a pattern it would repeat for the better part of two decades: ban, retreat, ban again, each cycle leaving more vehicles on the road than the one before. An inter-ministerial meeting banned the import and assembly of battery-powered three-wheelers in 2011, mainly due to electricity theft. In 2014, the High Court rejected five writ petitions from rickshaw owners seeking licences. It barred mechanised and battery-powered rickshaws from the streets. In 2015, the vehicles were ordered off twenty-two national highways. In 2021, the government announced another ban, and in December of that year, the High Court ordered a halt to imports. None of it held for long.

Then came 2024, when the whole cycle played out inside a single week. On 15 May, the road transport minister and both Dhaka mayors ordered the rickshaws off the capital's roads. Drivers poured into the streets of Mirpur and Agargaon; buses were vandalised, and a police box was set alight. Five days later, the ban was gone. The then prime minister, the minister explained, had allowed the vehicles to keep running out of concern for the poor, and the cabinet secretary added that the prime minister had not been aware of the ban in the first place. A decision taken by the transport ministry and two mayors was undone in under a week by a sentence from above.

After the political upheaval of August 2024, even the pretence of enforcement collapsed. One garage that had held ten or fifteen rickshaws before the uprising, news reports said, soon held about a hundred. In November, the High Court again ordered the vehicles off Dhaka's streets within three working days, this time on a petition from pedal-rickshaw owners; within a fortnight, the Appellate Division, at the interim government's own request, imposed a month's status quo while rules were drafted. The vehicles came back, as they always did.
A worker sorts through a large pile of discarded lead-acid batteries. The growing use of battery-powered rickshaws has raised concerns about lead pollution, particularly from the unsafe disposal and recycling of used batteries, posing serious risks to public health and the environment. Photo: Rajib Raihan

Why did none of it stick? An energy analyst quoted in the same report gave an honest answer: there is institutional interest in keeping the sector informal. Informality is where the money is. Drivers pay weekly sums to garage owners and, by many accounts, to the police; registration fees have also reportedly ended up in the pockets of local figures rather than the public treasury. A city corporation report cited in the press linked the illegal trade to a web of party men, associations and societies. A vehicle with no legal category pays rent to whoever controls the street. Legalising it threatens that arrangement, which is one reason legalisation took so long.

The costs that piled up in the dark

While government agencies remained divided over how to regulate battery rickshaws, the financial costs continued to mount. Electricity consumption became a particular concern because of the substantial revenue losses involved. Battery rickshaws draw around five per cent of the country's generated power, roughly 750 megawatts, much of it through illegal hooks thrown over power lines. Dhaka alone has tens of thousands of unlicensed charging points. The annual loss runs into thousands of crores of taka. That figure has been cited for years. The loss was allowed to continue because collecting the money would have meant admitting the fleet was real.

The quieter cost is lead. The batteries that power these rickshaws are the same lead-acid units that, once spent, are melted down in backyard furnaces across the country. UNICEF and Pure Earth ranked Bangladesh among the worst-affected nations on earth for childhood lead poisoning, with tens of millions of children carrying unsafe levels in their blood. E-rickshaw batteries account for the bulk of the country's lead-acid battery demand, and informal recycling of them is one of the leading sources of that exposure. A child does not have to ride a battery rickshaw to be harmed by one.

And then there are the crashes. BRTA's own data, compiled by the Centre for Policy Dialogue, attribute close to a fifth of road deaths in recent years to collisions involving these three-wheelers, the predictable result of putting an inadequately braked, overloaded frame into fast-moving mixed traffic. Professor Shamsul Hoque of BUET, who warned in 2011 that the vehicles could be useful only if introduced systematically, has since argued that the officials who enabled the problem by issuing approvals should be held accountable. Others have repeated the call in expert demands for a proper management roadmap. None has been held to account.
Battery-powered and conventional rickshaws crowd a road in Agargaon, Dhaka, contributing to severe traffic congestion. Years of inadequate regulation, coupled with the decline of public bus services, have allowed battery-powered rickshaws to become an increasingly important but poorly managed part of urban transport. Photo: Rashed Shumon

A fix that arrives late and reaches half the problem

The gazette of 29 October 2026 is, at last, a real attempt. Issued under a fresh amendment to the City Corporation Act, it makes registration mandatory: a QR-coded plate, a blue book, a five-year term. Every vehicle must carry a fitness certificate that meets BUET's safety standards, which means the brakes on all three wheels must be working. Manufacturers must be licensed against that design. Charging is confined to licensed points, and sellers must take back one old battery for every new one they sell and send it to an approved recycler. The vehicles are barred from highways, expressways and bus corridors, and capped at 25 kilometres an hour. On paper, almost everything the last twenty years lacked is here.

But the rules cover city corporations only, while the larger share of the fleet, perhaps fifty lakh vehicles, runs in municipalities and the countryside that the gazette does not touch. There is no cap on the number of machines and no timeline for retiring or converting the millions of non-compliant machines already on the road. A single national ID can register up to five vehicles, which, as urban planner Adil Muhammad Khan pointed out, favours the investor who owns a fleet over the driver who owns his livelihood. And enforcement rests with the same city bodies and police who have, for years, been named as the beneficiaries of the disorder. The secretary of a passengers' welfare group warned that if the number of licensed rickshaws continues to grow at the current rate, traffic in Dhaka and Chattogram could come to a standstill within a year.

The deeper problem is that the battery rickshaw was never the disease. It was the symptom. Dhaka's bus transport system has been in decline for decades: the share of city trips made by bus fell from about 28 per cent, according to JICA's 2009 household survey, to roughly 9 per cent, according to the 2023 urban transport plan. The city's franchise bus relaunch this month arrives mostly as old buses in new paint. Into that vacuum, where no reliable public transport reached the lane, the alley, the last kilometre home, the battery rickshaw arrived and stayed. When the formal system fails to move people, an informal one grows to do the job. Regulating the symptom while the buses still do not run is treating the cough and ignoring the lungs.

The battery rickshaw is not only a menace. It emits nothing from a tailpipe, it reaches places no bus will ever serve, and it supports the livelihoods of four million drivers, most of them poor. The economist Khondaker Golam Moazzem is right that it should not be made the sole scapegoat for congestion caused by private cars to a far greater extent. A fair accounting records that the vehicle met a genuine need the state declined to meet itself. That is why allowing these vehicles to operate without proper regulation for two decades has had serious consequences, and why assuming that the 2026 rules have resolved the problem risks repeating the same mistakes.

In Greek mythology, Pandora opens a box that releases suffering into the world, leaving only hope behind. Bangladesh opened its own Pandora's box around 2004 by allowing battery rickshaws to enter the market without a proper regulatory framework. As their numbers grew and problems multiplied, successive governments failed to address the consequences. More than two decades later, the authorities have introduced registration requirements without determining how many vehicles should ultimately be allowed on the roads. Whether the situation improves will depend on what happens next: developing reliable bus services and feeder routes so that battery rickshaws complement rather than replace public transport, extending regulations beyond city corporations, and gradually removing millions of unsafe vehicles from the roads. Without these measures, the new rules will amount to little more than damage control, leaving the underlying problems unresolved.

Dhrubo Alam is deputy transport planner at the Dhaka Transport Coordination Authority.

item.title: The Daily Star – Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq: Revisiting a complex legacy
item.description: One of the most influential political figures in the history of Bengal, Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq left an enduring legacy through his advocacy for peasant rights, his challenge to entrenched political and economic power, and his role in shaping the politics of colonial and postcolonial Bengal. Yet his political thought, achievements and contradictions deserve renewed attention beyond familiar historical narratives. Through a collection of essays and historical analyses, The Daily Star's Slow Reads revisits his life, political struggles, ideas and legacy, exploring how his vision and actions shaped Bengal's past and continue to resonate in Bangladesh today.

item.title: The Daily Star – The forgotten story of how Ekushey inspired language activism in West Pakistan
item.description:
The Bengali Language Movement of 1952 was not the only challenge to Pakistan's Urdu-centric language policy. Across West Pakistan, writers, intellectuals and political activists also resisted linguistic centralisation, demanding recognition for Punjabi, Sindhi and Pashto. Yet these movements differed in their political ambitions, strategies and relationships with the Pakistani state. In an interview with The Daily Star, French historian and writer Julien Columeau, author of Linguistic Resistance in Pakistan: Punjabi Language Movements After Independence (Columbia University Press, 2026), discusses this overlooked history, the influence of Ekushey February on Punjabi activists and the wider struggle for linguistic rights in Pakistan.

The Daily Star (TDS): What first drew you to the study of language movements and linguistic resistance in post-1947 Pakistan, particularly the Punjabi language movement?

Julien Columeau (JC): I have always been interested in language policy issues, especially the dichotomy between vernacular and national languages, undoubtedly because the region of France I come from predominantly spoke a vernacular language (Occitan), which was gradually replaced by French, both through the will of the state and due to people's negative attitudes towards their language, which they had been led to consider backward. A movement was launched to protect Occitan, but it did not achieve the desired results. After I moved to Pakistan, I found in Punjab an interesting situation, which reminded me to some extent of my own region. 

Without necessarily thinking, like Dr Olga Khokhlova, that Punjabi will die and be replaced by Urdu, one cannot deny that millions of Punjabi speakers are gradually switching to Urdu, and the gains obtained by activists remain symbolic, generating a paradoxical situation: Punjabi is not used as a medium of instruction in the province's schools, but one can do a PhD in Punjabi at university.

TDS: At the time of Partition in 1947, Urdu was the mother tongue of only about 3 per cent of Pakistan's population, while Bengali was spoken by more than 55 per cent. Why was Pakistan's ruling elite determined to establish Urdu as the sole national language?

JC: There are several factors, which I discuss in detail in my book, including the desire to merge linguistic and religious identity, and the fact that vernacular languages did not seem 'Islamic' enough in the eyes of activists like Baba-e-Urdu Maulvi Abdul Haq, who influenced the country's language policy: Bengali, with its vocabulary largely derived from Sanskrit and its script derived from Brahmi, did not appear Islamic enough to them, nor did Punjabi, which was labelled the 'language of the Sikhs'. 
Maulvi Abdul Haq (second from left), a prominent advocate of Urdu as Pakistan's national language. Following the Bengali Language Movement of 1952, he moderated his earlier position, acknowledging that the development of Urdu should not come at the expense of regional languages.

There was also a conviction among some activists that Urdu, even though it was the language of only 3% of Pakistanis, would become, within a few generations, the language of the majority, who would abandon their vernaculars in favour of Urdu, in the same way that the populations of North Africa, after being Islamised, had abandoned their vernaculars in favour of Arabic. Punjab, because of its elites' sympathy for Urdu and its pro-Urdu policies, seemed to these activists to be the province where this ‘great replacement’ of the vernacular language by the national language would have the best chance of taking place.

TDS: How did the government and the public in West Pakistan, particularly Punjab, react to the killing of students during the Bengali Language Movement on 21 February 1952?

JC: While the government's reaction was unanimously hostile, the public, at least in Punjab province, which is my subject of study, was divided. 

Left-wing circles were certainly shocked and outraged, and Ekushey rallied their solidarity with the Bengalis and their cause. Conservative circles had to acknowledge the Bengalis' determination to die for their language and that the inclusion of Bengali in the constitution was inevitable. 

Confronted with such determination, even a staunch activist like Maulvi Abdul Haq had to change his position regarding the unconditional imposition of Urdu: during the second Urdu conference held in Karachi only two months after Ekushey, he stated that the development of Urdu should not come at the expense of vernacular languages (whereas during the first conference in 1948, he had declared that none were worth developing).
Students prepare to defy Section 144 at Dhaka University's Old Arts Building on 21 February 1952. The Bengali Language Movement subsequently inspired Punjabi activists in West Pakistan, who began observing the anniversary in Lahore to press for recognition of their own mother tongue. Photo: Rafiqul Islam

TDS: Punjabi language activists later began observing 21 February in Lahore. How did the Bengali Language Movement influence their demands, strategies and understanding of linguistic rights?

JC: The Bengali movement inspired Punjabi activists by demonstrating that linguistic demands could mobilise public opinion and challenge the state's national ideology. It also showed that defending a vernacular language could be compatible with loyalty to Pakistan. However, Punjabi activists generally adopted more cautious demands. The position of Punjab's elites and the strong association between Urdu and Pakistani national identity constrained their ambitions. They sought greater recognition for Punjabi while avoiding accusations of undermining national unity, particularly through demands for constitutional recognition or an administrative role. The Punjabi activists adapted the Bengali example to their own political and ideological environment.
The cover of Linguistic Resistance in Pakistan: Punjabi Language Movements After Independence by historian Julien Columeau (Columbia University Press, 2026). The book explores the struggle for recognition of Punjabi and its connections with the Bengali Language Movement and wider linguistic resistance in Pakistan.

TDS: Punjabi activists were frequently accused of being anti-Pakistan or sympathetic to India and the Sikhs. How did they respond to these accusations while advocating recognition for their mother tongue?

JC: This accusation of being anti-national or anti-Pakistan weighed heavily on all Punjabi activists, regardless of their political affiliation. They were accused of being complicit with the Sikhs, who had been the main champions of Punjabi, and of wanting to diminish the role of Urdu. They therefore resorted to various strategies: to show that there was no antagonism between Urdu and Punjabi, they declared that Urdu descended from Punjabi (and, thus, serving the Punjabi cause was tantamount to serving the Urdu cause), or they proposed to Pakistanise Punjabi, purging it of lexical and cultural elements that could be identified as being linked to Sikhs, thereby promoting an Urduised version called Pak Punjabi. 

Others, finally, offered assurances that their movement would not go the Bengali way and that they were demanding neither that Punjabi be enshrined in the constitution nor that it be given the administrative role that belonged to Urdu.

TDS: Beyond East Bengal and Punjab, how did linguistic movements in Sindh and the North-West Frontier Province challenge Urdu's dominance? To what extent did these movements cooperate with Bengali activists?

JC: Punjabi activism formed part of a broader landscape of linguistic resistance. Strong movements also emerged in Sindh and the North-West Frontier Province, now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, associated with figures such as G. M. Syed and Bacha Khan. Their demands could be more radical than those of Punjabi activists, reflecting different regional histories and aspirations for cultural autonomy. Despite their strength, these movements achieved limited results in the early post-partition period. Symbolic recognition did not necessarily challenge Urdu's dominance in public institutions. Nor did regional movements consistently coordinate their efforts with the Bengali movement during the first years after independence. 

The creation of the National Awami Party (NAP) subsequently brought together political forces advocating regional rights and opposing centralisation, creating new possibilities for cooperation. These experiences demonstrate that shared linguistic grievances do not automatically produce solidarity; political alliances require organisation and the negotiation of different regional priorities.
Saadat Hasan Manto, the celebrated Urdu writer who reportedly considered writing in Punjabi. According to Julien Columeau, Manto even wrote a long story in Punjabi, but the manuscript was lost following his untimely death.

TDS: Despite their progressive political outlook, prominent Lahore-based writers such as Faiz Ahmad Faiz and Saadat Hasan Manto primarily wrote in Urdu. What explains their different attitudes towards writing in Punjabi?

JC: Faiz and Manto had very different temperaments, and their attitudes towards Punjabi were therefore different. Faiz was tempted in the early 1950s to write in Punjabi (he mentions this in a letter from prison to his wife) in order to communicate with the masses, but he gave up on the idea. It wasn't until the 1970s that he wrote a few poems in Punjabi. Safdar Mir and Ashfaq Tanwir Mirza attribute this renunciation of writing in Punjabi to a fear of social demotion, as writing in Urdu was a means of social and cultural advancement. 

Manto, on the other hand, even though he was an author who had made a name for himself writing in Urdu, did not seem to fear social demotion and reportedly considered embarking on a career as a Punjabi writer, even writing a long story in Punjabi. Unfortunately, his untimely death prevented him from realising this project, and his story has been lost.

TDS: How does examining the language movements of West Pakistan alongside the Bengali Language Movement help us better understand Pakistan's early history, particularly the relationship between language, national identity and political power?

JC: Studying Punjabi activism allows us to reconsider Pakistan's history beyond the dichotomy of an oppressive West Pakistan and an oppressed East Pakistan. Many intellectuals, writers and politicians in West Pakistan challenged their government's language policies and defended regional linguistic identities. Punjabi, Sindhi and Pashtun movements opposed aspects of linguistic centralisation, even if their demands and methods differed from those of Bengali activists. 
Pak Tea House in Lahore, a historic gathering place for writers, poets and intellectuals. The city's literary circles played an important role in debates over language, cultural identity and the dominance of Urdu in post-Partition Pakistan.

Pakistan's language politics should therefore be understood not simply as a confrontation between West and East Pakistan, but as a history of resistance within both regions. Ultimately, I believe the significance of West Pakistan's movements lies not only in their immediate achievements but also in the fact that they continued to challenge the government's assumption that national unity requires linguistic uniformity. Punjabi activism, despite its limitations, reveals how citizens and intellectuals contested linguistic hierarchies and imagined alternative relationships between language, identity and political community.

The interview was taken by Adrin Sarwar.
